document: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026)
body:
This sectoral National Risk Assessment considers the money laundering (ML), terrorist financing (TF) and proliferation financing (PF) risks arising from the use of Virtual Assets (VAs) and Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs) operating in, or from, the Isle of Man.
In summary, the assessment finds that:
The domestic VASP sector is small in scale but internationally exposed. In 2025, there were 19 registered VASPs, of which 4 were active, servicing approximately 1.3% of customers across all FSAreporting sectors. Despite its limited economic footprint, the sector is outward-facing, with the vast majority of customers and transaction flows linked to the UK and other overseas jurisdictions.
The assessment concludes that the VAs and VASP sector in the IOM presents a Medium ML risk, while TF and PF risks are assessed as Very Low. Residual risks are mitigated by the small domestic footprint, strong entry controls, and the absence of evidence of domestic terrorist or proliferation financing involving VAs.
ML risk is primarily driven by overseas predicate crime and cross-border activity. ML threats linked to VAs and VASPs are predominantly incoming and internationally generated, with limited evidence of significant domestic predicate offending involving VAs. Stablecoins, particularly USDT, feature increasingly in ongoing ML investigations and SARs, reflecting global typologies rather than domestic misuse.

chunk_id: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026), In this Assessment - 83498cdf7e1509f9
document: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026)
body:
VASPs operating in the Isle of Man do not offer privacy coins or other anonymity-enhancing services. However, 25% of registered VASPs permit, or intend to permit, transfers to unhosted wallets, creating exposure to risks arising outside the Island's regulatory perimeter.
Exposure to VAs in other regulated sectors is limited and controlled. Interaction between VASPs and banks, insurers and other financial institutions remains very low. Online gambling operators may accept VAs only under tightly controlled models that require conversion to fiat via regulated VASPs, with enhanced supervision applied.
The Isle of Man's AML/CFT/CPF framework materially mitigates inherent VA risks. VASPs are subject to registration, fit-and-proper requirements, risk-based supervision and inspection by the FSA, alongside mandatory business, customer and technology risk assessments. The introduction of the Travel Rule in 2024 and an enhanced supervisory approach have strengthened controls across the sector.

body:
Dan Davies Chair of the Financial Crime Strategic Board and Chief Officer of Home Affairs
I am pleased to introduce this risk assessment for Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers. This is a comprehensive sectoral report which addresses the risks associated with money laundering, terrorist financing, and proliferation financing for both the VASP sector and the use of VAs in the Isle of Man. The Financial Crime Strategic Board (FCSB) would like to extend its thanks to regulators, law enforcement agencies, government departments and representatives from industry, notably the VASP sector. Their support in producing this assessment, including those who contributed through targeted engagement and data gathering, has been invaluable. Special thanks are also extended to XReg Consulting for their valuable expertise throughout this process.
Since the publication of the last National Risk Assessment in 2020, the VA landscape has evolved rapidly. Global adoption of VAs has increased, technology has advanced significantly, and new and sophisticated financial crime threats have emerged. These threats relate directly to VAs but also reflect an increasingly sophisticated approach to criminality more broadly.

body:
International criminals have sought to exploit the inherent features of VAs such as anonymity, the speed of cross-border transfers, and inconsistencies in global regulatory frameworks. These developments have tested the adaptability of supervisors, law enforcement and industry in equal measure.
Despite these challenges, the response from the Isle of Man authorities, and the sector itself has been strong and proactive. The FSA has enhanced its supervisory approach, strengthened its expertise, continued proactive engagement with the sector, introduced the "Travel Rule" requirements, and deepened its understanding of VA related risks. Collaborative work with law enforcement, including increased use of blockchain analytics and multi-agency investigations and asset seizures, has further strengthened the Island's resilience. These efforts have led to improved controls, better risk identification, and a more mature and robust compliance culture across active VASPs.
Although the registered VASP sector remains small relative to other parts of the financial services industry, it continues to form an important component of the Isle of Man's innovation driven economy. The sector contributes positively to technological development and supports wider digital transformation efforts across financial and professional services.

chunk_id: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026), 2. Executive summary - 1afb3d4174401a2f
document: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026)
body:
This executive summary outlines the principal findings from the Isle of Man's first standalone VA and VASP sector ML/TF/PF Risk Assessment. It complements the broader National Risk Assessment framework and reflects updates in global standards, supervisory expectations and technological developments since the last 2020 ML/TF NRA.
The VASP sector remains very small in economic terms but plays an important role within the Island's digital and financial ecosystem. The sector mainly serves non-resident customers and provides custody and administration services, VA-to-VA and VA-to-fiat exchange and brokering through OTC or dealer-type models. The sector is defined in Section 3, including details of active VASPs and ancillary VA-related exposure in other regulated industries.
Internationally, it is observed that Offshore Virtual Asset Service Providers (oVASPs) present a wide range of risk profiles, influenced by differences in regulatory maturity, market development, sector composition, and the scale of cross-border financial activity. At the same time, the nature of VAs themselves, including their mobility, speed of transfer, anonymity-enhancing features and rapid innovation cycle means the risk landscape evolves more quickly than in traditional financial services.

chunk_id: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026), 2. Executive summary - 6a0bdcf75c9011b4
document: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026)
body:
Domestically, it is important to note that VASPs on the Island are subject to the AML/CFT Code, which prohibits anonymous business relationships. Agencies are not aware of any domestic VASPs offering privacy-enhancing VA products or anonymity-focused services.
The emerging risks have intensified in a fast-moving, technology-driven environment. Criminal groups increasingly exploit advanced technologies cyber-attacks, phishing, malware, spoofed or synthetic identities, chain-hopping, mixers/tumblers and exploitation of VAs within broader fraud ecosystems. These trends intersect with complex business models, including relationships involving oVASPs, online gaming operators, payment service providers and unregulated third-party platforms. A notable risk is the rapid establishment of VA-related operations using pre-packaged or outsourced business models, enabling criminals to create the appearance of legitimacy, obtain banking relationships, and move illicit funds across multiple jurisdictions with limited scrutiny.
This risk assessment provides a substantially more detailed evaluation of these risks and represents a significant enhancement from the 2020 ML/TF NRA, incorporating improved data, new threat intelligence, supervisory insights and revised World Bank methodology specific to VAs and the VASP sector.

body:
Sector Size and Activity: As at December 2025, 19 VASPs were registered in the Isle of Man, with 4 active providers. Domestic VASP‑related activity forms only a minimal proportion of national income, however, its linkages to other material sectors, particularly online gambling, banking and TCSPs as well as contributing to financial flows in and out of the Island, means ML risks remain present.
The majority of the VASP sector services relates to exchange and brokerage-type activity, and some domestic VASPs are connected to wider group structures overseas. Certain VA-related businesses (e.g., software developers, technical service providers) fall outside international AML/CFT/CPF standards, though their supporting infrastructure such as banking and TCSPs, sit firmly within the regulated perimeter.
Most domestic VASPs make use of professional services, particularly Isle of Man-regulated TCSPs, to fulfil key roles such as directors, MLROs, principals or operational managers. This introduces dependencies and potential vulnerabilities, such as structural opacity or concentration of control, examined further in Section 8.

document: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026)
body:
The Financial Services Authority (FSA) has a VASP registration process in place which mandates that a VASP entity maintains a real presence on the Island. The FSA has implemented a risk-based supervisory framework in relation to the AML/CFT/ CPF supervision of VASPs, which includes thematic reviews, assessment of Travel Rule implementation, and risk-based supervisory inspections.
International Profile: The vast majority of VASP customers and nearly all transaction flows are international which is in line with the other financial services and DNFBP sectors and the IFC nature of the Isle of Man. The majority of customers are resident in the UK, followed by the IOM, although in terms of domestic customers exposure is minimal. Other countries where customers are resident include Australia, Italy and France. This international footprint heightens exposure to foreign predicate crime and cross-border laundering risks.
Risk Assessment: Under the revised VAs and VASPs World Bank methodology published in late 2025, overall VAs (as a product) and domestic VASPs (as a sector) present a Medium ML risk level; this has decreased since the assessment in the last 2020 NRA. However, the threat level remains elevated due to the emerging risks and overseas predicate crime, assessed as Medium High.

chunk_id: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026), Key Highlights from the Assessment - 240a3cdf00e31247
document: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026)
body:
Where exposure to VAs arises only indirectly, for example, when online gambling operators use VASPs to convert VAs into fiat, the risk is lower. These transactions are smaller in volume and take place within a tighter, highly regulated licensing framework.
TF and PF risks in the VASP sector remain assessed as Very Low, reflecting the limited scale of confirmed cases. TF risks mainly relate to the potential use of VASPs for small cross-border donations, peer-to-peer transfers, unhosted wallets and anonymity-enhancing features that reduce traceability. PF risks stem from the possible misuse of VASPs to evade sanctions through rapid cross-border transfers, links to high-risk jurisdictions and reduced visibility over counterparties in complex or foreign VASP arrangements.
Inherent Vulnerabilities: The inherent vulnerabilities relating to VAs and VASPs is Medium. This derives from the rapid movement of value across borders, non-face-to-face relationships, the features of VAs such as the potential to obscure transaction and identity and the use of unhosted wallet activity which also carries greater exposure.

body:
Supervisory and Legal Framework: The Isle of Man maintains a comprehensive legal and supervisory framework for VASPs, building on the previous NRA and previous positive mutual evaluations.
The Island's AML/CFT/CFT framework was further strengthened following the 2016 MONEYVAL review, notably through expanded sanctioning powers relating to identified deficiencies relating to preventative measures and controls in respect of AML/CFT/CFP and the enhancements made to the Gambling and AML/CFT Codes where relevant and associated guidance for the sector. The FSA also introduced Travel Rule requirements from 2024.
The GSC permits online operators to accept VAs through VASPs. Which must be subject to regulation to FATF standards., Activity is concentrated in stablecoins and no exposure to privacy coins. Operators with VA exposure are classified as higher risk and therefore subject to enhanced AML/CFT/CPF controls, including specific guidance outlining the need for blockchain-analytics capabilities, and increased monitoring.
Further information on detailed sector characteristics is included in Section 3.
Summary of Proposed Actions: This risk assessment identifies a number of areas for improvement; these are aligned to the strategic aims from the National Financial Crime Strategy 2024-2026. Future actions should focus on enhancing risk understanding, strengthening collaboration and improving the Island's capability to identify and mitigate emerging threats within the VA ecosystem.

Public sector and industry work together to achieve a common goal of meeting international standards. See Sections 3. Introduction and 8. Inherent Vulnerabilities

- The IOMFCP groups should consider undertaking work to understand VA-specific risks, formalising intelligence-sharing arrangements, and expanding outreach to operators and professional services sectors on new typologies and technology risks.

chunk_id: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026), 3. Introduction - 0cd7e2b212f60433
document: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026)
body:
As an established IFC, the IOM is exposed to ML/TF/PF threats that arise from predicate offences that take place outside the IOM. As with most IFCs, previous NRAs (including the most recent 2026 NRA) have highlighted that the services provided in the IOM may be used to conceal the proceeds of crime or to conceal or disguise the origins of those proceeds, through international transfers of funds and in some instances, the use of complex corporate structures. In line with many of the Island's sectors, the VASPs' customer base is predominantly non-resident, mostly from the UK, which means that activities and transactions that result in funds being linked to the Island largely take place outside the jurisdiction.
International criminals are increasingly looking to exploit vulnerabilities in VAs and VASPs to launder the proceeds of crime or to fund terrorist activities and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction. This report assesses the threats and vulnerabilities relating to both VAs and VASPs in the IOM, including the exposure to VAs in other sectors, and the effectiveness of the mitigating controls in place at both a national and service providers' level.

chunk_id: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026), 3. Introduction, How Industry Should use this Report - 3020ad82a0cd8e25
document: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026)
headers: How Industry Should use this Report
body:
Businesses in the regulated sector, and those subject to registration requirements are obliged to undertake and maintain a Business Risk Assessment (BRA) which must have regard to any relevant findings of the most recent NRA relating to the Island. Therefore, industry must be able to show how they have considered and mitigated the relevant risks identified in this report.

Given a number of NRAs are being published over several months, it is acceptable to consider each NRA as it is published but update the overall BRA at its next formal review date. Consideration should be given to the Customer Risk Assessment (CRA) and Technology Risk Assessment (TRA) and if these require updating.

Given the interconnected nature of VAs with other material sectors including banking, TCSPs and online gambling, the FCSB encourages all regulated financial institutions and designated businesses to consider the implications of this assessment for their own operations. Entities with indirect or occasional exposure to VAs should likewise consider whether updates to internal controls are required. A high-level summary of the findings of this report is also included in the Money Laundering NRA.

chunk_id: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026), 3. Introduction, Methodology - dabc35b26aeb13cd
document: Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers National Risk Assessment (April 2026)
body:
In developing the methodology to apply for this risk assessment, consideration has been given to guidance issued by several international institutions, including the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the World Bank (WB) and the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI). The Island has applied the WB methodology when carrying out its broader risk assessment and the sectoral assessment of other sectors.
This Risk Assessment uses the revised WB methodology, published in late 2025, to assess the ML and TF risks posed by VAs and the domestic VASP sector. The revised tool allows for a tiered approach, to cater for jurisdictions at varying stages of capacity and market development. Based on the criteria provided, the IOM has used the "intermediate" tier.
The methodology takes account of the overall ML and TF threats, the vulnerabilities relevant to VAs and the VASP sector in the IOM and assesses the effectiveness of the controls in place to mitigate the risks, including the legal, supervisory and law enforcement framework, and the AML/CFT/CPF controls in place by the sector and other sectors with VA exposure in the IOM.
Data, statistics, and information used for completing the risk assessment tool modules, as well as findings, interpretation, and judgement under the scope of the Risk Assessment, completely belong to the IOM authorities and do not reflect the views of the World Bank Group.

The VASP sector in the IOM remains small relative to the financial services sector, with 19 VASPs on the FSA register
(end of December 2025) out of which four are operational, and one firm reported that it was in the process of dissolving the company. Inactive firms are often firms incubating business ideas or building technical back‑office systems and processes before offering to customers, these firms are still required to abide by all the AML/CFT/CPF controls within the jurisdiction and still form part of the oversight framework and engagement model.

The main services offered by Isle of Man VASPs include VA custody and administration, VA-to-VA exchange, VA-to-fiat exchange, and receiving or transmitting orders for virtual assets.

From the 46k customers reported in 2024, approximately 85% were rated by VASPs, according to their internal customer risk profiling methodologies, as standard risk customers, while 12% were rated as low risk. The increase in the volume of drugs being smuggled into the IOM from the UK by OCGs is reflective of the higher street prices available, the value of which needs to be realised. VAs can provide an alternative to cash and traditional financial services for OCGs to move the proceeds of crime and integrate them into the traditional financial system. Although there is evidence of OCGs increasingly purchasing high-value goods with the illicit funds in the IOM, VAs are not widely accepted in the IOM for goods and services and there is no evidence of VAs being exploited in this way. There is however evidence of criminal proceeds in VAs being converted to fiat, which is then being used to purchase high value goods on Island.

Assessing TF threats requires consideration of each of the recognised stages; the collection, movement and use of funds.
From a geographical perspective, the Island is situated between the UK and the Republic of Ireland and is away from globally recognised conflict zones and higher-risk jurisdictions. The IOM has never experienced a domestic terrorist attack. No terrorist groups or cells are believed to be active or present on Island.
The more likely exposure to TF for IFCs, including the IOM, arises from their high levels of cross-border business, particularly complex transactions, and the international activities of their charities and other non-profit organisations (collectively, NPOs), with the attendant possibility of the services and products offered by IFCs or assets raised and/or disbursed by their NPOs being used by parties outside the jurisdiction to fund terrorism abroad. No operators have applied to handle VAs directly to date or have been denied permission. Of the transactions involving VAs linked to these operators, 90% were in stablecoins (USDT and USDC).

The vulnerability of such operators in dealing with VAs is somewhat mitigated by the fact that operators are only allowed to deal with VASPs that are registered or licensed and comply with FATF Standards.
Operators with exposure to VAs are treated as Medium High or high risk by the GSC and therefore subjected to increased supervision.
The inherent vulnerability of gaming operators with exposure to VAs has been assessed as Medium High. However, given the effectiveness of the controls both at operator level and at a national level, the final risk level has been scored as Very Low.

Under the AML/CFT Code 2019, obliged entities (which includes all FSA licensed and registered entities) are mandated to undertake several risk assessments, including a business risk assessment, customer risk assessments, technology risk assessment. The business and technology risk assessments must be undertaken as soon as reasonably practicable after the entity commences business, while the customer risk assessment must be performed prior to establishing a business relationship or undertaking an occasional transaction with or for a customer.
As part of its registration process, the FSA undertakes a Fit and Proper (F&P) Person test to ensure that all individuals involved in the operation of the VASP meet the Authority's F&P expectations. This involves the review of Personal Questionnaires and, in some cases, interviews to further ascertain an individual's competence and integrity.
Registrations are considered on a case-by-case basis and may be granted with or without specific conditions attached. Once registered, the registration remains effective until revoked or until the person is de-registered.
To assist applicants seeking registration as Designated Businesses, the FSA issued guidance under section 9(6) of the DBRO Act in the form of the Designated Businesses Registration Policy (DBRP).
Additionally, under the AML/CFT Code 2019, an MLRO must be appointed and will be treated as a specified person.

Similarly, proposed changes to a registered Designated Business' ownership structure may require prior notification to the FSA in line with section 19 of the DBRO Act.
When part of a group, the FSA may request information about other group entities from the applicant, other regulatory authorities, and the group entities in question.

Like Financial Institutions, Designated Businesses must submit an AML/CFT Return on or before 31 March every year, which, at a minimum, must include a declaration as to the extent to which the registered person meets the requirements of AML/ CFT/CPF legislation.
The FSA has the power to carry out inspections and investigations, which may include inspecting books, accounts and documents, and investigating transactions at a registered Designated Business' premises to assess the extent to which it meets the requirements of the DBRO Act and the applicable AML/CFT/CPF legislation, as well as the Designated Business' Policies and Procedures to comply with the DBRO Act and relevant AML/CFT/CPF legislation.

body:
Online gambling operators are licensed under the Online Gambling Regulation Act 2001, which defines online gambling as:

- any gaming, where any player enters or may enter the game or take or may take any step in the game, by means of an electronic communication;

- the negotiating or receiving of any bet by means of an electronic communication; or

- any lottery in which any participant acquires or may acquire a chance by means of an electronic communication.

The licensing process involves stringent fit and proper checks on beneficial owners and controllers, as well as source of funds and source of wealth (SOW) checks. Where the SOW derives from VAs, the GSC undertakes enhanced checks which include a VA-audit by an approved party. Applicants are also required to submit their AML/CFT/CPF policy, BRA, CRA and TRA, and appoint a suitably qualified MLRO and AML/CFT/CPF compliance officer, all of which are reviewed and considered by the GSC before granting a licence.

Regarding operators' exposure to VASPs, the guidance issued by the GSC to date requires that operators dealing with VASPs only do so where those VASPs are subject to appropriate AML/

CFT/CPF measures as required by the FATF. The assessment to determine whether this is the case is undertaken by each operator. The suitability of the assessment carried out by the operator is then checked by the GSC as part of its onsite inspections.

Typology Scenario
Victim D responds to a social media advertisement advertising large returns should the individual choose to buy virtual assets through the seller. Victim D contacts Perpetrator D for more information and chooses to purchase GBP 500.00 of virtual assets. Victim D sends the funds to Perpetrator D via bank transfer. Fraud

Perpetrator E is in the process of moving the administration of his business from another country to the Isle of Man. During the onboarding process the corporate service provider conducts enhanced due diligence on the business owner. When they receive this documentation, they notice that a large part of Perpetrator E's wealth was generated through the sale of cryptocurrency. The corporate service provider requested a copy of Perpetrator E's tax return for the country he was tax resident in for the year of the sale. They noted that the cryptocurrency sale was not declared on the tax return. In that country profits of cryptocurrency sales over a prescribed amount are subject to income tax. By failing to declare the sale Perpetrator E was suspected to be evading tax. The corporate service provider reported this to the FIU.
Tax crimes
Lack of reporting of cryptocurrency assets held, sales, or profits to central tax authorities in certain countries can be considered evasion of tax.
Typology Scenario
Perpetrator F owns an IT security company who are based on the Isle of Man. They sell IT security services to various companies around the world. They bank with a bank on the Isle of Man. All funds they receive into the account originate from payment service providers who utilise virtual IBANs. The bank on the Isle of Man identified the payment flows were in excess of expected activity.

body: The bank conducted a client review of Perpetrator F's IT security company. They identified adverse media for some of the clients of the company linking them to cryptocurrency scams and human rights violations. Investigation of the payment service providers identified they dealt in the conversion of virtual assets or were part of a group that undertook this function. The bank requested invoices for Perpetrator F's clients. These invoices were extremely basic in nature and the breakdown of services provided was extremely generic. The amounts charged for these services appeared excessive. The bank noted the majority of the funds received were transferred to various group companies and there was a lack of expenditure for staff salaries given the size of the operation and for the purchase of additional IT infrastructure. The bank was suspicious they were receiving the proceeds of crime originating from on chain cryptocurrency crime and this was being layered/laundered by Perpetrator F's IT security company. The bank suspected Perpetrator F's company were using the guise of providing essential services and receiving payment for these services to launder large amounts of criminal funds generated on the blockchain.

body: Indirect VA exposure All of the banks on the Isle of Man do not directly accept cryptocurrency. Due to the lack of knowledge around cryptocurrency and the organisations that enable the conversion of virtual assets to Fiat currency, banks can unknowingly accept the proceeds of crime through a financial institution directly involved with the conversion of cryptocurrency, or a financial institution a few steps removed. These financial institutions may have weaker controls. Virtual IBANs are commonly used to further layer funds. Organised criminals may exploit this process to launder the proceeds of crime on a large scale, generated or laundered using the blockchain.
